deities: Lord Shiva as Triambakeshwar (Jyotirlinga; unique three-faced linga representing Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesh; the linga is said to be eroding over time from continuous water contact)
Goddess Ganga (Godavari) — worshipped at Kushavarta kund
Lord Brahma (puja of the Brahma face of the linga)
Nandi (large Nandi before the temple; marble Nandi inside)
festivals: Maha Shivaratri (biggest annual festival, huge pilgrim crowds)
Simhastha Kumbh Mela (held every 12 years at Trimbakeshwar-Nashik; one of the four Kumbh sites)
Shravan Maas (heavy rush on Mondays; the gem-studded crown is displayed to devotees on Mondays, traditionally said to date to the Pandava era)

history.dynasty: Peshwa (Maratha confederacy); construction commissioned by Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb), continued under his successors; Kushavarta kund built by Sardar Raosaheb Parnerkar, Fadnavis of Indore State
history.period: Present temple built 1755–1786 (work begun December 1755, Margashirsha; completed in 1786 after 31 years, at a reported cost of 16 lakhs); earlier temple destroyed by Aurangzeb
history.summary: The Trimbakeshwar Temple at Trimbak, about 28 km from Nashik city, is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Lord Shiva and the only one where the linga has three faces — representing Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesh — worshipped as a single deity. Legend says the sage Gautama, whose prayers brought the Ganga down from Brahmagiri as the Godavari after he inadvertently killed a cow, trapped the river's first flow in the Kushavarta kund and requested Shiva to reside there, so Shiva manifested as the linga. The earlier temple was destroyed by Aurangzeb; the present black-basalt structure in Hemadpanthi/Nagara style was built by Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) between 1755 and 1786. The deity was once adorned with the world-famous Nassak Diamond, appropriated by the British during the Third Anglo-Maratha War. Trimbakeshwar is the origin point of the Godavari, the second-longest river of India, and a major centre for rituals such as Narayan Nagbali, Kaal Sarp Dosh Shanti, Tripindi Shraddha and Rudrabhishek. It is also one of the four sites of the Simhastha Kumbh Mela.

name: Trimbakeshwar Temple
town_description: Trimbak (also spelled Tryambak) is an ancient pilgrimage town in Nashik district, Maharashtra, about 28 km from Nashik city at the foothills of the Brahmagiri hill (Nilgiri and Kalagiri nearby). The Brahmagiri range is the source of the Godavari river, and the town's Kushavarta kund is regarded as the symbolic origin of the river. Trimbakeshwar is the seat of one of the twelve Jyotirlingas and hosts the Simhastha Kumbh Mela every 12 years, making it one of Maharashtra's most important Shaivite pilgrimage centres.

travel.airport: Nashik Ozar Airport (ISK, approx. 37–55 km depending on route; limited flights — verify). Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (approx. 170–180 km, 4–5 hours by road) is the better-connected option; taxis and buses available from both.
travel.railway: Nashik Road Railway Station (code NK, approx. 36–40 km), well connected to Mumbai, Pune, Delhi, Chennai and Hyderabad; taxis and buses run from the station to Trimbak.
travel.road: Trimbak is approx. 28 km from Nashik city (NH160); frequent MSRTC state buses run from Nashik's Central Bus Stand, plus private taxis and cabs. Mumbai is approx. 170–180 km away (via NH3 to Kasara, then State Highway 21).

visitor_information.best_time: September to March for pleasant weather. Maha Shivaratri and Shravan Mondays are the most vibrant but most crowded times; the Simhastha Kumbh Mela (every 12 years) draws enormous crowds.
visitor_information.opening_hours: Daily approx. 5:30 AM to 9:00 PM (verify — some sources list 5:00 AM opening / 9:30 PM closing). General darshan is free (a free Darshan Entry Pass may be required); a priority/Donation Darshan pass costs about Rs. 200 per person (verify current fee). Key pujas: Brahma Puja 7:00–8:30 AM, Mahadev Puja 10:45 AM–12:30 PM, evening puja/aarti 7:00–8:30 PM. Men entering the garbhagriha for abhishek must wear a dhoti without shirt/vest; women should wear saree/traditional attire; modest clothing for general entry; footwear and photography restricted inside the sanctum.
